messages.subject: saving Stan models so that they don't need to be recompiled, with these saved from one R session to the next
parts:
Hi all.  For our lm/glm/lmer/glmer/etc replacement, we want to have precompiled models.  Bob was saying it is difficult to do this in R, that there’s some problem so the precompiled models can’d be saved.  But see the attached file and note from Sebastian.   It looks like maybe this can be done?
A

Begin forwarded message:

From: "Weber, Sebastian" <sebasti...@novartis.com>

Attached is an r snippet which caches a Stan model. If you execute the script with Rscript stanCache.r for the first time it will compile and save the Stan model. When called the second time, it will just load the compile model from the hard disk and run it without recompiling, i.e. a lot faster.

messages.subject: Re: saving Stan models so that they don't need to be recompiled, with these saved from one R session to the next
parts:
You still need to have rstan installed (from source) in order to use those binary models, so that wouldn't solve our installation problems. It would help in the sense that it obviates the need for every user to (inefficiently) write their own regression model. But we would have to make each binary model for both Windows and Mac (and possibly every variant thereof). The approach I was taking with the rstanarm package was to create the binary models once when the package was installed, which accomplishes about the same thing. In principle, we could split the rstan package into two one which had stanc and the stuff you need to compile a .stan model and one with the class definitions and stan(), sampling(), optimizing(), traceplot(), etc. Then, people could execute models someone else wrote even if they couldn't or wouldn't compile anything. But the most universal approach would be to use the intermediate representation of LLVM to distribute models that can be run in Chrome or any browser if they were converted to javascript via emscripten. That would allow people to do models without compiling or even being able to do R or Python. The compilation part mostly works now but we need a browser-based interface to call a CmdStan model.

Ben

parts:
B

No, the point of this was not to solve our installation problems. Rather, I’m looking forward to the day soon when we will be able to do MLE and penalized MLE (and marginal MLE and penalized marginal MLE for hierarchical models) in general in Stan.  At that point, I’d like preprogrammed versions of lm, vlm, bayesglm, lmer, glmer, bglmer, polr, bayespolr, etc.  The idea is that regular R users will be able to just run our lm etc functions by default.

So we would not need to make the binary models.  Rather, our R package would come with a function such as lm_stan_setup() that would compile all the models and save them on the user’s own computer.

Also I’d like this to be all do-able in Python, because another one of my goals is to allow people who don’t use R to fit any statistical model they might want to fit.

A

messages.subject: Re: saving Stan models so that they don't need to be recompiled, with these saved from one R session to the next
parts:
To be clear:  there would be 2 functions (or one function with 2 options) for any of these models:
- option 1:  point estimation.  Basically, Stan’s using its optimizer to mimic the classical program
- option 2:  full Bayes:  Stan’s doing full Nuts.
I’d like to have both options.  Option 1 has the advantage (compared to Stan’s option 2) of being fast, deterministic, and directly comparable to well-understood methods and the advantage (compared to simply running lm or whatever) of being general, scalable, allowing arbitrary priors and messy models (a particular issue with lmer/glmer when there are many variance components), and being written in Stan so immediately generalizable to full Bayes.

messages.subject: Re: saving Stan models so that they don't need to be recompiled, with these saved from one R session to the next
parts:
The optimizing() function has a hessian argument that if TRUE returns the Hessian on the unconstrained space. It is up to the user to negate and invert (which might not be possible numerically) draw from a multivariate normal and convert to the constrained parameter space. So, it is less than fully automatic, but it is doable. The stuff with MML and doing more models is all on the Stan side.

Ben

all the higher-order auto-diff in place. That's probably going to make
it slow in high dimensions. I think we can probably live with the accuracy
of finite diffs. Marcus also said that we could potentially pull a Hessian
out of BFGS.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: saving Stan models so that they don't need to be recompiled, with these saved from one R session to the next
parts:
On Tuesday, February 25, 2014 1:10:47 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
The Hessians must be done with finite differences because we don't have
all the higher-order auto-diff in place.  That's probably going to make
it slow in high dimensions.  I think we can probably live with the accuracy
of finite diffs.  Marcus also said that we could potentially pull a Hessian
out of BFGS.

That is what optimizing() is doing now, numerical differentiation of the auto-differentiated gradient function in the unconstrained space. Once we have higher-order auto-diff, we can swap that piece out. The final inverse Hessian approximations of quasi-Newton methods are not super-accurate I don't think but at least they are positive definite and already inverted.

Ben
